title: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
goal: By the end you can replace constructor calls with named static or companion factories that check their input and return sealed results, pass factories around as functions, and group matching products behind an abstract factory.
opening:
Walk into the town bakery and ask for "a loaf for sandwiches". You don't name a recipe, and you don't pick an oven. The baker hears what you need and decides: today it's the white tin loaf. Next door, the furniture maker takes orders for dining sets. Ask for one in oak, and the table and the chairs come from the same workshop, so they match.

Code makes objects all day, usually with `new`, which names the exact class every time. That's fine until the choice depends on something: the weight of a parcel, a setting, whether we're in a test. Then the `new` calls spread through the program, each one deciding on its own, and one day a parcel booked with one courier gets tracked with the other.

In the last lesson, a private constructor and one `getInstance()` decided how many objects exist. In this lesson, we'll let a factory decide which object you get: static factories with names, factory methods passed around as functions, factories that return a sealed result instead of throwing, and an abstract factory for a set that must match. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `List.of(1)` and `List.of(1, 2, 3)` both return a `List<Integer>`. What do you expect `getClass()` to say for each?
options: Both are `ArrayList`
Both are the same private class
Two different private classes, chosen by the factory from the number of elements
`List` itself, since `List.of` is defined on the interface
warmup.why: `List.of` is a static factory, so it can return any class it likes. In JDK 21 it returns `List12` for one or two elements and `ListN` for more, both private. A constructor could never do that: `new X()` always gives you an `X`. And an interface can't be created at all, so `List` itself is impossible. The first section shows the JDK's factories choosing, with real output.

sections.h: Static factory methods: constructors with names
sections.body:
Start with the counter at the bakery. You say what you want, and the baker hands over something that fits. You never see the kitchen. A **static factory method** is that counter in code: a static method that returns an instance of its class, or of some class behind an interface. Effective Java, the best-known book of Java advice, opens with it (item 1: consider static factory methods instead of constructors). The JDK, the libraries that come with Java, is full of them: `List.of`, `Duration.ofMinutes`, `Integer.valueOf`, `Thread.ofVirtual`.

A constructor can do one thing: make a new object of exactly its own class. A static factory can do four things a constructor can't.

1. It has a name. `Duration.ofMinutes(2)` and `Duration.ofSeconds(2)` both take a `long`. Two constructors with the same parameter types can't exist, and `new Duration(2)` would say nothing anyway.
2. It can return an object it made earlier. `Integer.valueOf(100)` hands back the same cached object every time.
3. It can return any subtype, chosen from the input. `List.of(1)` and `List.of(1, 2, 3)` return two different private classes. `EnumSet.noneOf` picks a set backed by a single `long` when the enum has 64 constants or fewer, and a bigger one otherwise.
4. The class it returns doesn't have to exist when the factory is written. JDBC, in `java.sql`, is Java's standard way to talk to a database, and each database company ships its own driver. `DriverManager.getConnection(url)` returns a connection from whichever driver on the classpath (the list of places the JVM loads classes from) accepts the URL, and those drivers were written long after `java.sql`.

The warm-up was the third point. `FactoriesInTheJdk`, in the Try it, asks each factory what it handed back. On JDK 21 it printed:

```text
List.of(1)            -> List12
List.of(1, 2, 3)      -> ListN
EnumSet of TimeUnit   -> RegularEnumSet (7 constants)
EnumSet of scripts    -> JumboEnumSet (164 constants)
```

Same method, different classes, and you can't write any of those class names in your own code. The factory is the only door.

The downsides are small. A class with only private constructors can't have subclasses, which pushes you toward composition (building a class out of other objects instead of extending one) and costs little. Factories are also harder to spot than constructors, so stick to the usual names: `of`, `from`, `valueOf`, `parse`, `newX`, `create`.

For the shop's own value types, make this the default. Picture a `Price` with a private constructor and two doors, `Price.ofCents(450)` and `Price.parse("4.50")`. With the constructor private, every `Price` in the program went through your checks. The compare block at the end of this lesson writes it out in both languages.

**A constructor can only say `new`. A factory can say what you mean, and choose.**

A static factory makes its choice inside its own class. The next step moves the choice out, away from the code that uses the object.

try.title: Watch the JDK's factories choose
steps: Read `FactoriesInTheJdk`. For each of the first four lines, predict the class name you'll see. The Kotlin twin adds three lines for Kotlin's own `listOf`.
Run it from the `labs/` folder with the command below.
Type `RegularEnumSet` in your editor, as if you wanted to use it. Can you?

code.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.java

alt.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.patterns.l02

import java.time.Duration
import java.util.EnumSet
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

// The same JDK factories called from Kotlin, plus Kotlin's own. Predict each class name first.

fun main() {
    // JDK static factories pick an implementation from the input
    println("List.of(1)            -> " + java.util.List.of(1).javaClass.simpleName)
    println("List.of(1, 2, 3)      -> " + java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3).javaClass.simpleName)
    println("EnumSet of TimeUnit   -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit::class.java).javaClass.simpleName +
            " (" + TimeUnit.entries.size + " constants)")
    println("EnumSet of scripts    -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript::class.java).javaClass.simpleName +
            " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.entries.size + " constants)")

    // Kotlin's factory functions do the same (full names, since two of these are nested classes)
    println("listOf()              -> " + listOf<Int>().javaClass.name)
    println("listOf(1)             -> " + listOf(1).javaClass.name)
    println("listOf(1, 2, 3)       -> " + listOf(1, 2, 3).javaClass.name)

    // a factory can hand back a cached instance, and its name says what you get
    println("Currency EUR twice    -> same object? " + (java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR") === java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR")))
    println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2))
}

try.expect: `List12` for one element and `ListN` for three. `RegularEnumSet` for `TimeUnit` (7 constants) and `JumboEnumSet` for `Character.UnicodeScript` (164 constants on JDK 21). Both `same object?` lines print `true`, because the factories handed back cached objects. None of these classes is public, so your editor won't let you name them: the factory is the only door. Kotlin's `listOf` plays the same game, returning `EmptyList`, `Collections$SingletonList` or `Arrays$ArrayList` depending on how many elements you pass.

sections.h: Factory Method: let someone else choose the class

aside.title: Does my framework write factory methods for me?
aside.body: If you write web services, it probably calls them. In Spring, a method marked `@Bean` builds an object; in Quarkus, a method marked `@Produces` does the same. The framework calls that method and passes the result to every class that asks for the interface, so the rest of the code never names the concrete class. The framework calls it when it creates the object, not once per request. A choice that depends on the current request, such as the weight of this parcel, still needs a factory you call yourself.

compare.title: A checking factory that returns a sealed result

java.title: Price.java

kotlin.title: Price.kt

compare.note: The shape is the same in both: a private constructor, named factories, a sealed result and an exhaustive `switch` or `when` at the call site. Java 21 takes the result apart with record patterns (`case Price.Ok(Price p)`), and Kotlin smart-casts it, treating it as that type once `is` has checked it. The real difference is where the factory lives. Kotlin has no `static`: `ofCents` is a function on the companion object, so Java callers would write `Price.Companion.ofCents(...)` without `@JvmStatic`. Kotlin also gives you `operator fun invoke` and top-level factory functions, and its named arguments remove a lot of the constructor confusion that pushes Java code toward factories in the first place.

worked.title: Replace look-alike constructors with named factories

steps.say: The shop's `Delivery` class grew four constructors: an order can go to the door or be collected in the shop, with or without a note. Look at the last line and decide what it creates before reading on.
steps.code:
public class Delivery {
    public Delivery(String orderId, int grams) { ... }                 // to the door
    public Delivery(String orderId) { ... }                            // collect in the shop
    public Delivery(String orderId, int grams, String note) { ... }    // to the door, with a note
    public Delivery(String orderId, String note) { ... }               // collect, with a note
}

new Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm");   // ?
steps.alt_code:
class Delivery {
    constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int) { ... }                   // to the door
    constructor(orderId: String) { ... }                               // collect in the shop
    constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String) { ... }     // to the door, with a note
    constructor(orderId: String, note: String) { ... }                 // collect, with a note
}

Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm")   // ?

steps.say: It's a collection with a note, but only the parameter types say so. Adding delivery to a neighbor would mean a fifth constructor with yet another mix of types. Give each kind a name, check there, and make the constructor private so every `Delivery` goes through a factory.

Later in the day, a parcel for the door needs a van and a collection needs a shelf behind the till. When the kinds behave differently, let the same factories return different records (or data classes) behind a sealed interface. Callers don't change, and code that handles deliveries can switch over the two cases with the compiler checking it covers both. In Kotlin, `@JvmStatic` keeps `Delivery.collect(...)` working for Java callers, and Kotlin callers could also write `Delivery.ToDoor(orderId = "o-2", grams = 2_500, note = "blue gate")`: named arguments already remove the confusion that started this.

lab.title: A parcel factory, a courier family, and shipping that only knows interfaces
steps: Open the three files. `Parcel` is a parcel that knows its weight and its courier, `CourierServices` is the family of a courier company's two services, and `Shipping` books a parcel for an order.
Run the tests. All nine fail with `NotImplementedError`, the error Kotlin's `TODO()` throws.

Write `Parcel.parse` in `Parcel.kt`. Apply the three checks from its KDoc comment (Kotlin's documentation comment) in order, and return `ParcelResult.Invalid(reason)` with the exact reason strings. Only `parse` may call the private constructor.

Write `CourierServices.forCourier`. One private class built from settings (courier, company name, prefix) can serve both families. Use `require` for the checks that refuse to mix couriers, and an exhaustive `when` with no `else`.
Write `Shipping.ship` as a `when` over `Parcel.parse(weight)`. Call `servicesFor` only for a valid parcel.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: `raw.trim().split(" ")` gives you the number and the unit. `toDoubleOrNull()` returns `null` for text that isn't a number, and `roundToInt()` (import `kotlin.math.roundToInt`) turns `2500.0` into `2500`.
Multiply kilograms by 1,000 before you round: "2.5 kg" is 2,500 g. Check `grams <= 0` after rounding, so "0 g" and "-1 kg" both give `weight`.
`Booker` and `Tracker` are `fun interface`s, so `Booker { parcel, orderId -> ... }` builds one from a lambda.
`require(condition) { "message" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` when the condition is false.

drill.title: A sealed-result factory from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In Kotlin (or Java, with a static `parse`), write `Email` with a private constructor and a companion `parse(raw: String): EmailResult`. It returns `Ok(email)` when the trimmed text has exactly one `@` with something on both sides, and `Invalid(reason)` otherwise. Then write a caller that uses `when` (or `switch`) with no `else` or `default`.

alt.title: Java

recap: A static factory is a constructor with a name. It can return a cached object or any subtype, and pick the class from its input (`List.of`, `EnumSet.noneOf`, `DriverManager.getConnection`).
Make the constructor private and check the input in the factory, so every instance in the program is a good one.

The GoF Factory Method, a subclass that overrides a creation hook, is now usually a `Supplier<T>` or `() -> T`, often a constructor reference such as `FakeMessenger::new`. A factory's `switch` or `when` over a sealed type or enum gets no `default` or `else`.

Kotlin factories live in the companion object, in `operator fun invoke`, or in a top-level function named like the type (`Job()`, `MutableStateFlow(0)`). Return a sealed result for answers callers must handle.
Abstract Factory makes a family of matching products from one choice, so callers can't mix one courier's booker with another's tracker.
The limit: an abstract factory makes new families cheap and new products expensive, because adding a product changes the interface and every family.
closing:
We started at the bakery counter and the furniture maker's workshop. In code, the counter became a static factory with a name, and the baker's choice became a function passed in. The workshop became one interface that makes a matching booker and tracker, and the compiler checked every switch.

Now search your own code for `default ->` or `else ->` in a `switch` or `when` that creates objects. Each is a place where a new case slips through without a word. If the type is sealed or an enum, delete the branch and see what the compiler says.

Next, we'll meet objects with many optional parts. When a constructor needs ten arguments, how do you build one that anyone can read?

quiz.q: Which of these can a static factory do that a constructor can never do?
options: Return an instance of a subtype chosen from its arguments
Check its arguments
Be called from another package
Throw a checked exception
quiz.why: Constructors can check their arguments, be public and throw checked exceptions too. Only a factory can return a cached object or a different class, like `List.of` returning `List12` or `ListN` depending on how many elements you pass.

quiz.q: A factory has `switch (channel) { case SMS -> ...; case EMAIL -> ...; default -> new FakeMessenger(); }`. A teammate adds `POST`, for letters by post, to the enum. What happens?
options: A compile error in the factory
A `MatchException` at run time
Notices by post silently go to the fake messenger
The switch throws `NullPointerException`
quiz.why: The `default` branch catches every new constant, so the build stays green and letters by post go to the fake. Without `default`, a switch expression over an enum must cover every constant, and adding `POST` would be a compile error at exactly this line.

quiz.q: Which Kotlin shape lets callers write `Fee(250)` while you return a cached instance?
options: A secondary constructor
`operator fun invoke` in the companion object
An `init` block
A `data class` with a default argument
quiz.why: A constructor always makes a new object, primary or secondary. `operator fun invoke(cents: Int): Fee` on the companion turns `Fee(250)` into a function call that can return anything, including a cached instance. Readers expect a new object from that syntax, so use it with care.

quiz.q: You have `interface CourierServices { Booker booker(); Tracker tracker(); }` with a bike family and a van family. Now you need a `Canceller` product too. What does that cost?
options: Nothing: add one new class
Only the van family changes
You have to switch to Factory Method
The interface and every existing family change
quiz.why: Abstract Factory makes new families cheap and new products expensive: every family must now produce a canceller, including any fake family your tests use. Weigh that before you add a product to the interface.

quiz.q: From lesson 1 of this track: a Kotlin `companion object` holds a factory `of(...)` and `val cache = loadPrices()`. When does `loadPrices()` run?
options: When the outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer
Lazily, the first time `cache` is read, under a lock
Every time `of` is called
At program startup, for every class on the classpath
quiz.why: A companion object is initialized when its outer class is loaded, which matches a Java static initializer, so `loadPrices()` runs then even if nobody reads `cache`. If you want it on first read, write `val cache by lazy { loadPrices() }`.

flashcards.front: Name two things a static factory can do that a constructor can't.
flashcards.back: Return a cached instance, and return a subtype chosen from its arguments (`List.of` gives `List12` or `ListN`). It also has a name.

flashcards.front: Why leave out `default` in a factory's switch over a sealed type or enum?
flashcards.back: So adding a new case is a compile error at the factory. With `default`, the new case silently takes the default branch.

flashcards.front: What replaced the GoF Factory Method's creator subclass in modern Java?
flashcards.back: A function: a `Supplier<Messenger>`, usually written as a constructor reference such as `SmsMessenger::new`.

flashcards.front: Kotlin has no `static`. Where does a class's named factory usually live?
flashcards.back: In its `companion object`: `companion object { fun parse(raw: String): ParcelResult }`.

flashcards.front: What name may a Kotlin factory function have, by the coding conventions?
flashcards.back: The same name as the abstract type it returns, like `fun Job(): Job` or `MutableStateFlow(0)`.

flashcards.front: When should a factory return a sealed result instead of throwing?
flashcards.back: When the failure is an answer the caller is expected to handle, like a mistyped weight. Keep exceptions for bugs and broken machinery.

flashcards.front: Abstract Factory: what is cheap to add, and what is expensive?
flashcards.back: A new family is cheap (one implementation). A new product is expensive (the interface and every family change).

terms.plain: A static method that returns an instance, used instead of a public constructor.
A creation hook that lets something other than the caller pick the concrete class. Now often a `Supplier<T>` or `() -> T`.
An interface that creates a whole family of matching objects, with one implementation per family.
Objects that must be used together, such as one courier company's booker and tracker.
A sealed set of answers (`Valid`, `Invalid`) returned instead of throwing. A `switch` or `when` must handle every case.
A Kotlin object tied to a class, and the usual home for that class's factories.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why `CourierServices.forCourier(courier)` has no `else` branch, and why `Shipping` takes a `(Courier) -> CourierServices` instead of calling `forCourier` directly.
explain_back.answer: With no `else`, the `when` has to name every `Courier`. When someone adds `CARGO_BIKE`, the factory stops compiling until they decide which family it gets, instead of quietly falling into a default. The function parameter keeps `Shipping` from knowing which families exist and how they're built. The real program passes `CourierServices::forCourier`, and a test passes a lambda that returns a fake family and records which courier was asked for. So the choice of concrete classes lives in one place, and the shipping logic can be tested without any courier at all.

deeper.body:
`DriverManager` is a factory whose products didn't exist when it was written. On first use, it asks `ServiceLoader` for every `java.sql.Driver` that a JAR on the classpath lists in a `META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver` file. `getConnection(url)` then offers the URL to each driver until one accepts it. You can build the same plug-in mechanism yourself: define an interface, list the implementations in `META-INF/services/<interface name>`, and call `ServiceLoader.load(YourInterface.class)`. The module system adds `provides ... with ...` and `uses ...` declarations for the same thing.

Effective Java lists the usual factory names, and sticking to them makes factories easy to find: `from` for a one-argument conversion (`Date.from(instant)`), `of` for gathering several values (`EnumSet.of(...)`), `valueOf`, `getInstance` or `instance`, `create` or `newInstance` when each call returns a new object, `getType` and `newType` when the factory lives in another class (`Files.newBufferedReader`), and a bare `type` (`Collections.list`).

From Java, a Kotlin companion factory is `Price.Companion.parse(...)`. Mark it with `@JvmStatic` and Java callers can write `Price.parse(...)`. If Java code uses your Kotlin library, do it for every public factory. The same goes for `@JvmOverloads` on functions with default arguments, which you'll meet in *Builder and Prototype* (lesson 3 of this track).
